chunks: Muhammad ibn Harun al-Zanjani informed me, saying: Ali ibn Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, from Abu Ubayd, that he said: I heard several from the people of knowledge say:

The Anwaa' are twenty-eight stars known for their rising times during the seasons of the year, all from summer, winter, spring, and autumn. In every thirteenth night, one star sets in the west with the rising of dawn, and another rises opposite to it in the east at that same time, and both are known and designated. The completion of all these twenty-eight coincides with the completion of the year, then the matter returns to the first star with the commencement of the coming year. The Arabs in the Jahiliyyah (Age of Ignorance), when one of them set and another rose, would say: 'There must be wind and rain at that time,' and they would attribute every rain that occurred at that time to that star which set at that moment, saying: 'We were rained upon by the rising of Thuraiya, Dabran, Samak,' and whatever of these stars.

Based on this, these are the Anwaa', and one of them is a 'Naw''. It was named 'Naw'' because when the setting star sets in the west, the rising star rises in the east with its rising, and it 'Naw'' (rises/turns away), and that rising is the 'Naw'', so the star was named by it. And so is everything that rises and moves with slowness, it 'Naw'' at its rising. He, Blessed and Exalted is He, said: 'That he might burden the band of the strong'.

key_terms.الأنواء: The lunar mansions or twenty-eight stars used for astronomical and meteorological predictions.
key_terms.الثريا: The Pleiades star cluster, one of the prominent stars in the Anwaa'.
key_terms.الجاهلية: The Age of Ignorance, the pre-Islamic period in Arab history.
key_terms.الدبران: Al-Dabaran (The Follower), a bright star in the Taurus constellation.
key_terms.السماك: Al-Simak (Aldebaran or similar), a star used in ancient Arab astronomy.
key_terms.نوء: A term meaning rising, turning away, or the specific event of a star's rising/setting.

ai.seo_question: What are the Anwaa' (lunar mansions) and how did pre-Islamic Arabs associate them with weather?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records this definition of 'Anwaa'' (lunar mansions) to clarify the pre-Islamic meteorological beliefs where specific stars were thought to cause rain, a concept the Quran later critiqued. The text elucidates the astronomical mechanism of these twenty-eight stars rising and setting in pairs, linking the linguistic root 'naw'a' (to rise or turn) to the Quranic phrase 'litnaw'a' to demonstrate how language evolved from celestial observation to theological discourse.

en.basel-kadem: I was informed by Muhammed bin Harun al-Zanjani, that he said: We were told by Ali bin Abdul-Aziz, from Abu ‘Ubaid, that he said: I heard several from the people of knowledge say:

Anwaa’ are twenty-eight stars whose visibility is known throughout the times of the year, all from the summer, winter, spring and autumn. In every thirteenth night of it, one star of it falls during the sundown along with the rise of dawn, whereas another star appears opposite to it in the east of its hour, and both are known and recognized. The ending of all these twenty-eight is with the ending of the year, and then the matter returns to the first star by the commencement of the coming year. The Arabs, during the Jahiliya, used to say, when one star of them falls and another star appears: «It must be that there comes wind and rain along with that» and so they would ascribe every rain therein to that star that falls therein, and they would say: «Our rain is due to the movement towards the west  of Thuraiya, Dabran, Samak» and whatever would be of these stars.

Based on this, that is anwaa’ [1], and one is a naw’. It was only named naw’ because if a faller of them falls during sundown, that which appears in the east at sunrise comes up. It appears in an appearance , and that emergence is naw’, and so the star was named with it. So it is with everything that emerges and moves in slowness, it performs naw’ at its emergence. He, Blessed and Exalted is He, said: «would burden the band consisting of the strong» [28:76]
